item.title: Kibitsu Shrine: The 400-Metre Corridor and the Momotaro Legend — Guide
item.description: Kibitsu Shrine, on the Kibi Plain west of Okayama city, is one of the most distinctive shrines in western Japan. Its main hall, rebuilt in 1425 and designated a National Treasure, has a rare twin-gabled roof form found nowhere else, called kibitsu-zukuri. From it, a covered wooden corridor runs some 400 metres along the contour of the hillside, rising and falling through the trees in a receding perspective that is unforgettable.

item.title: Matsue Castle: A Black Original Keep by the Lake — Guide
item.description: Matsue Castle, completed in 1611, is one of just twelve original castle keeps surviving in Japan and one of only five designated National Treasures. Unlike the many concrete reconstructions elsewhere, this is the genuine wooden building, its dark plank walls earning it the nickname the ‘black castle’ or ‘plover castle’. Rising five storeys above the city between Lake Shinji and Lake Nakaumi, it has a defensive, unadorned strength, and the climb up its steep internal stairs is rewarded with a view over the lakeside town.

item.title: Sofukuji Temple — Guide
item.description: Sofukuji, in the hills of central Nagasaki, is one of Japan’s finest and most colourful Chinese temples, founded in 1629 by the city’s Chinese residents from Fujian province. Belonging to the Ōbaku school of Zen — introduced to Japan from China in the seventeenth century — it is built in an authentic southern-Chinese Ming-dynasty style quite unlike Japanese temples, and vividly evokes Nagasaki’s role as Japan’s great port of Chinese trade.

item.title: Usuki Stone Buddhas — Guide
item.description: The Usuki Stone Buddhas (Usuki Sekibutsu), in a quiet valley near the town of Usuki in eastern Oita, are the finest group of cliff-carved Buddhist images in Japan and one of the country’s great religious art treasures. Some sixty stone figures were carved directly into the soft volcanic tuff cliffs from around the Heian and Kamakura periods (roughly the 12th century), grouped into several clusters along the hillside. Remarkable for their number, scale and outstanding artistic quality — with serene, beautifully modelled faces, some still retaining traces of original colour — they were the first stone-carved works in Japan to be designated National Treasures.

item.title: Himeji Castle: Japan's Finest Surviving Castle — Guide
item.description: Himeji Castle is the greatest surviving castle in Japan and one of the finest in the world: completed in its present form in 1609, it escaped the fires, sieges, demolition orders and wartime bombing that destroyed almost every other Japanese castle, and stands today entirely original. Its brilliant white plastered walls and layered gables earned it the nickname Shirasagi-jo, the White Heron Castle, and its defensive design — a spiralling maze of gates, walled lanes and dead ends climbing to the six-storey keep — is as impressive as its beauty.

item.title: Taisanji Temple: A National Treasure in Kobe's Western Hills — Guide
item.description: Taisanji sits in a forested valley in Kobe’s Nishi Ward, far enough from the city that most visitors never hear of it — which is a pity, because its main hall, rebuilt in 1293 after a fire, is a designated National Treasure and one of the finest medieval buildings in the Kansai region. The wooded grounds hold a vermilion three-storey pagoda, an Important Cultural Property gate, sub-temples and a strolling garden, and the surrounding valley turns brilliant with maples in late autumn.

item.title: Hikone Castle: A National Treasure Above Lake Biwa — Guide
item.description: Hikone Castle, completed in 1622 by the Ii clan — hereditary retainers of the Tokugawa — is one of just twelve castles in Japan to keep its original keep and one of only five designated National Treasures. The elegant three-storey tower, built partly from materials salvaged from defeated rivals' castles, crowns a hill of spiralling ramparts, plunging stone walls and trick gates above the eastern shore of Lake Biwa, and its foot holds the strolling garden of Genkyuen, whose ponds and teahouse borrow the keep itself as scenery.

item.title: Inuyama Castle: Japan's Oldest Original Keep — Guide
item.description: Inuyama Castle, completed in 1537 on a bluff above the broad Kiso River, holds what is generally considered Japan’s oldest surviving original castle keep, one of only a dozen that escaped demolition, fire and war — and one of just five designated National Treasures. Climbing its steep, creaking wooden stairs is a walk through unrestored history that ends on a top-floor balcony with sweeping views over the river to the mountains of Gifu, and each spring several hundred cherry trees ring the castle hill and the old town below, making the season’s festival the prettiest time to visit.

item.title: Matsumoto Castle: Japan's Oldest Five-Tiered Original Keep — Guide
item.description: Matsumoto Castle, nicknamed ‘Crow Castle’ for its striking black exterior, is one of Japan’s most important original castles and a designated National Treasure, its five-tiered keep dating to the late 16th century and standing as one of the oldest surviving original keeps in the country. Unlike hilltop castles, it sits on flat land surrounded by a wide moat that mirrors the black-and-white keep, and the scene is especially memorable when framed by cherry blossoms in late April or lit up during seasonal night illuminations reflecting on the still water.

item.title: Zuiryuji Temple: A National Treasure Zen Complex in Takaoka — Guide
item.description: Zuiryuji Temple was built in the mid-17th century by Maeda Toshitsune, second lord of the powerful Kaga domain, to honour his father and predecessor, and today stands as one of the finest surviving examples of early Edo-period Zen temple architecture in Japan. Its main hall, sanmon gate and dharma hall are all designated National Treasures, connected by covered corridors in a symmetrical layout characteristic of formal Zen temple design, offering visitors a rare chance to walk through a complete, historically intact temple complex.

item.title: Osaki Hachimangu: Sendai's National Treasure Shrine — Guide
item.description: Built by Date Masamune in 1607, Osaki Hachimangu is one of Japan’s most elegant shrine buildings — a National Treasure clad in gold lacquer and vivid black urushi lacquerwork, blending Momoyama-period opulence with subdued Zen restraint. The long approach through an ancient cedar grove creates a quiet transition from the modern city outside. Every January the shrine hosts the Dontosai festival, and each November families bring children for Shichi-Go-San blessing ceremonies.

item.title: Shiramizu Amidado: A Heian-Era National Treasure Temple — Guide
item.description: Shiramizu Amidado, built in 1160 by the widow of a regional lord to pray for her late husband’s soul, is a National Treasure and one of only a handful of surviving Heian-period Pure Land Buddhist temple gardens in Japan. The hall sits on an island in a lotus pond, meant to evoke the Buddhist paradise of the Pure Land, with the wooden structure and its seated Amida Buddha reflected serenely in the water — a rare, intact glimpse of 12th-century religious architecture.
